title: macOS security for defenders
summary: How Macs defend themselves and how defenders watch them: signing, Gatekeeper, notarization, XProtect, SIP, TCC, launchd persistence, unified logs, Endpoint Security, MDM, FileVault, and real stealer cases.
outcomes: Read codesign, spctl and syspolicy_check output and explain what a signature, Team ID and notarization prove
Explain when Gatekeeper and XProtect run, and why pasted Terminal commands skip both
Explain how SIP, the signed system volume and FileVault protect the OS and data, and how Shrootless bypassed SIP
Describe TCC consent and the mechanism and fix of CVE-2020-9934, powerdir and the XCSSET bypass
Find and triage launchd persistence and dylib injection risks with plists, codesign and the hardened runtime
Use the unified log, Endpoint Security events and osquery tables to detect stealer and persistence activity
Plan fleet controls with MDM, Automated Device Enrollment, PPPC and declarative management
Investigate and respond to Atomic Stealer and 3CX-style compromises on Macs

lessons.title: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app

blocks.md:
Picture one ordinary afternoon on a company Mac. Someone downloads `Notes-Setup.dmg` (a disk image file, the usual way Mac apps are shipped) from a search ad, opens it, types their password into a dialog, and gives the new app access to their Documents folder. Each of those steps passes a different macOS control, and each control answers a different question.

This course walks that path as a defender: what each control checks, what it does not check, how real attackers slipped past, and what evidence each step leaves for you. You know from the prerequisite course how a kernel, a reference monitor and a sandbox work. Here we apply that to the operating system that runs most tech-company laptops.

**The kernel.** macOS runs on XNU, part of Apple's open source Darwin operating system. Apple's [XNU repository](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu) says the name is an acronym for "X is Not Unix" and describes XNU as a hybrid of the **Mach** kernel from Carnegie Mellon University, parts of **FreeBSD**, and **IOKit**, a C++ API for drivers. The same repository has a `security` directory for mandatory access check policy interfaces: the hooks that SIP (System Integrity Protection, lesson 6) and the sandbox use, the macOS version of the reference monitor idea.

**Mach-O** (Mach object) is the executable file format, the macOS counterpart of Linux's ELF (Executable and Linking Format).

blocks.title: The questions macOS asks, in the order a download meets them

nodes.label:
May it run at all?
Gatekeeper, notarization

What may it do?
hardened runtime, sandbox

Can it touch the OS?
SIP, signed system volume

What did it do?
Endpoint Security, logs

scenes.caption: A file arrives from the internet. Nothing has run yet. The first questions are about trust: who signed it, and has Apple scanned it?
XProtect checks the code against Apple's malware signatures at first launch. Apple calls Gatekeeper, notarization and XProtect its layers for preventing launch and blocking known malware.
Once running, the process is limited by how it was signed (hardened runtime) and by the sandbox, then must ask the user (TCC) before reading protected data.
Even as root it cannot rewrite the operating system: SIP and the signed system volume protect the OS itself.
Across all of it, defenders observe through Endpoint Security and the unified log, and set policy on every Mac through mobile device management (MDM). The rest of the course takes each box in turn.

blocks.md:
Apple's [Platform Security guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/protecting-against-malware-sec469d47bd8/web) structures malware defence in three layers:

1. **Prevent launch** of malware: the App Store, or Gatekeeper combined with notarization.
2. **Block** malware that reaches a Mac from running: Gatekeeper, notarization and XProtect.
3. **Remediate** malware that has run: XProtect.

Notice what is missing: nothing in that list stops a user from typing a command into Terminal, or from handing their password to a convincing dialog. Those gaps are where most real Mac compromises of the last few years happened, and they are why defenders need visibility (lessons 11 to 13) as well as prevention.

"Macs don't get viruses" is a myth defenders still meet. Information stealers such as Atomic Stealer (lesson 16) have been sold to criminals as a monthly service since 2023, and Microsoft documented new campaigns delivering them to Macs in 2026. The built-in controls are strong, but they mostly decide what may *launch*; social engineering goes around them.

Each macOS control answers one question. When you investigate a Mac incident, ask which question the attacker never had to face: was the code never quarantined, was it signed and notarized, did the user approve a prompt, did it run as a script rather than an app?

blocks.question: A user pastes a command from a web page into Terminal, and it downloads and runs a shell script. Which layer from Apple's three-layer model was designed to stop this first step?
options: Prevent launch: Gatekeeper and notarization check the script before it runs
SIP, because the script runs as the user
TCC, because Terminal is a protected app
None of them directly: the three layers are built around apps and files, so a typed command skips the launch checks
blocks.explain: Gatekeeper and notarization evaluate apps and files that arrive with quarantine. A command typed by the user is the user acting. Later layers (XProtect behaviour rules, TCC, logging) may still catch what the script does, which is why defenders need more than launch checks.

blocks.question: Which statement about XNU is supported by Apple's own source repository?
options: It is a pure microkernel with every driver in user space
It combines Mach from Carnegie Mellon with FreeBSD components and the IOKit driver API
It is the Linux kernel with Apple patches
XNU stands for "Extended NeXT Unix"
blocks.explain: Apple's XNU README describes a hybrid kernel: Mach plus FreeBSD components plus IOKit, and expands the acronym as "X is Not Unix".

lessons.title: Code signing: what a signature on a Mac proves

blocks.md: Start with a tiny program. On a Mac with Apple silicon we compile a two-line C file and ask `codesign` what it sees. We never signed it ourselves, yet it already has a signature: Apple's [Big Sur release notes](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-big-sur-11_0_1-universal-apps-release-notes) state that on Apple silicon "the operating system enforces that any executable must be signed before it's allowed to run", and that "a simple ad-hoc signature is sufficient". The linker adds that ad hoc signature for you.

blocks.code:
% cat hello.c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { puts("hello from a toy app"); return 0; }
% clang -O2 -o hello hello.c && ./hello
hello from a toy app
% codesign -dv ./hello
Identifier=hello
Format=Mach-O thin (arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20400 size=382 flags=0x20002(adhoc,linker-signed) hashes=9+0 location=embedded
Signature=adhoc
Info.plist=not bound
TeamIdentifier=not set
Sealed Resources=none
Internal requirements=none
blocks.caption: Real output, macOS 26 on Apple silicon (the Executable= path line is omitted). Signature=adhoc: hashes but no certificate, so no identity.

blocks.md:
**What is inside a signature.** The core is the **Code Directory**: a list of hashes, one per page of the executable (`hashes=9+0` means nine page hashes and no special slots here). The hash of the Code Directory itself is the **cdhash**, a fingerprint of exactly this code. A real signature then signs the Code Directory with a certificate; an **ad hoc** signature has the hashes but no certificate.

Because pages are checked as they are loaded, changing one byte breaks the match. The `kill` flag you will see on real apps means, in `codesign`'s manual, that code "will die when it becomes dynamically invalid".

blocks.title: Page hashes in the Code Directory catch one changed byte

scenes.caption: Signing hashes every page of the executable and stores the list in the Code Directory. Hash values here are shortened, illustrative labels, not real SHA-256 output.
We overwrite one byte in page 4 of a copy. Its hash no longer matches the stored one; every other page still matches.
When the kernel maps the changed page it finds the mismatch and kills the process. In the real run below the tampered copy died with exit status 137 (128 + 9, SIGKILL).

blocks.prompt: We copy `hello`, overwrite one byte in the middle of the copy with `dd`, and run the copy. What happens on Apple silicon?
blocks.reveal: `codesign --verify` reports `invalid signature (code or signature have been modified)`, and running it prints nothing: the shell reports exit status 137, which is 128 plus signal 9, SIGKILL. The kernel killed the process when the modified page failed its hash check. On Apple silicon every native executable must carry a valid signature, even an ad hoc one.

blocks.code:
% codesign -dvv "/Applications/Google Chrome.app"
Identifier=com.google.Chrome
Format=app bundle with Mach-O universal (x86_64 arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20500 size=765 flags=0x12a00(kill,restrict,library-validation,runtime) hashes=13+7 location=embedded
...
Authority=Developer ID Application: Google LLC (EQHXZ8M8AV)
Authority=Developer ID Certification Authority
Authority=Apple Root CA
...
Notarization Ticket=stapled
...
TeamIdentifier=EQHXZ8M8AV
...
% codesign -dvv /bin/ls
Identifier=com.apple.ls
...
Platform identifier=26
...
Authority=macOS Software Signing
Authority=Apple Code Signing Certification Authority
Authority=Apple Root CA
...
TeamIdentifier=not set
...
blocks.caption: Real output, trimmed with .... A third-party app signed with a Developer ID certificate, and an Apple platform binary.

blocks.md:
Read the **Authority** lines bottom-up: a chain from Apple Root CA down to the signing certificate. Three kinds of signer matter to defenders:

- **Apple platform code** (`macOS Software Signing`, a `Platform identifier`, no Team ID): part of the OS.
- **Developer ID**: a certificate Apple issues to a registered developer to distribute outside the App Store. The **Team ID** (here `EQHXZ8M8AV`) is, per Apple's guide, a 10-character alphanumeric string tied to that developer account; it is the most useful single field for allowing or blocking a vendor.
- **Ad hoc**: no identity at all, only integrity.

Apple's [guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/app-code-signing-process-sec3ad8e6e53/web) separates the two jobs: code signing proves the developer's software "hasn't been tampered with since the developer built and signed it"; notarization (lesson 4) proves Apple scanned it.

A valid signature says *who* built the code and that it is unchanged. It does not say the code is safe. Attackers sign malware with Developer ID certificates obtained under real or stolen identities, and in the 3CX case (lesson 17) the vendor's own build system signed the trojanised app.

blocks.question: A binary shows `Signature=adhoc` and `TeamIdentifier=not set`. What can you conclude?
options: It was notarized by Apple
Its pages match the stored hashes, but no certificate ties it to any developer
It is an Apple platform binary
It cannot run on Apple silicon
blocks.explain: Ad hoc means integrity without identity: the Code Directory hashes exist, but nothing is signed with a certificate. Apple silicon accepts ad hoc signatures for running locally, so it can run; it just tells you nothing about who made it.

blocks.question: You want an allowlist rule that keeps working when a vendor ships a new version of its app. Which field is the best match?
options: The Team ID from the signing certificate
The cdhash
The file's SHA-256
The file name
blocks.explain: A cdhash or file hash changes with every build. The Team ID stays the same across all of that developer's signed releases, which is why allowlisting tools such as Santa (lesson 12) and MDM policies support it.

lessons.title: Quarantine and Gatekeeper: the first-launch check

blocks.md:
Gatekeeper is not a scanner that watches every file. It is a check at a specific moment, triggered by a specific marker. Apple engineer Quinn "The Eskimo!" of Developer Technical Support explains it in [Resolving Trusted Execution Problems](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/706442): when Safari downloads a zip archive it sets the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute (a piece of metadata stored alongside the file); Archive Utility copies that marker to the files it unpacks; and "running a quarantined app always invokes Gatekeeper".

The same post lists what does **not** quarantine: "Unix-y networking tools, like `curl` and `scp`, don't quarantine the files they download", and `tar` and `unzip` do not pass quarantine on to what they unpack.

blocks.code:
% xattr -l Toy.app
com.apple.provenance:
% ditto Toy.app Downloaded-Toy.app
% xattr -w com.apple.quarantine "0083;6b046560;Safari;" Downloaded-Toy.app
% xattr -l Downloaded-Toy.app
com.apple.provenance:
com.apple.quarantine: 0083;6b046560;Safari;
% spctl --assess --type execute -vv Downloaded-Toy.app
Downloaded-Toy.app: rejected
% spctl --assess --type execute -vv "/Applications/Google Chrome.app"
/Applications/Google Chrome.app: accepted
source=Notarized Developer ID
origin=Developer ID Application: Google LLC (EQHXZ8M8AV)
blocks.caption: Real output on a toy app built in a scratch folder. We set the quarantine attribute by hand to imitate a browser download (Apple: not API; apps use quarantinePropertiesKey). Never opened. spctl rejects the unquarantined Toy.app too; quarantine decides whether Gatekeeper runs at launch.

blocks.md:
`spctl` (its manual page is titled "SecAssessment system policy security"; SecAssessment is the system policy API it drives) asks the same policy engine Gatekeeper uses. Our ad hoc toy is **rejected**: it has no Developer ID and no notarization. Chrome is **accepted** with `source=Notarized Developer ID`.

`syspolicy_check distribution` runs, in its manual's words, "the same checks on your app as macOS does when determining if your app can be executed", and explains failures:

```
% syspolicy_check distribution Toy.app
App has failed one or more pre-distribution checks.
Adhoc Signed App      Severity: Warning
Notary Ticket Missing Severity: Fatal
```

(real output, condensed). The `com.apple.provenance` attribute fits another line in Apple's [guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/gatekeeper-and-runtime-protection-sec5599b66df/web): Gatekeeper "also tracks the provenance of files written by downloaded software".

blocks.title: One download, one first launch

scenes.caption: The browser saves the download and marks it with com.apple.quarantine (which app, when).
The user double-clicks the app. Because it is quarantined, the system invokes Gatekeeper before any of its code runs.
Gatekeeper checks the Developer ID signature, that the code is unaltered, and the notarization ticket (stapled, or looked up online), plus revocations.
All good: Gatekeeper still asks the user once, so a file posing as a document cannot run code silently.
A file fetched with curl has no quarantine. Opening it never reaches Gatekeeper at all. This is the gap paste-and-run attacks use.

blocks.md:
**Overrides.** Apple's [developer news of 6 August 2024](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=saqachfa) announced that in macOS Sequoia (15) "users will no longer be able to Control-click to override Gatekeeper when opening software that isn't signed correctly or notarized"; they must go to System Settings, Privacy & Security, and click Open Anyway. On macOS 15 or later the Endpoint Security API reports these overrides as an event (`gatekeeper_user_override` in `eslogger`), so a fleet can log every one.

**Translocation.** Apple's guide also says that when necessary Gatekeeper opens apps "from randomized, read-only locations", so a malicious plug-in shipped next to a benign app is not loaded automatically.

**Policy.** Managed Macs can restrict users to App Store apps, or App Store plus identified developers, and block the override; MITRE ATT&CK tracks bypass attempts as [T1553.001 Gatekeeper Bypass](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/001/).

Gatekeeper is a first-launch, quarantine-triggered check. Removing the attribute (`xattr -d`), fetching with `curl`, or running a script through `bash` or `osascript` means it is never asked. Treat a process tree of browser or chat app, then Terminal, then curl, then shell or osascript as a detection signal, not as something Gatekeeper already covered.

blocks.question: An attacker's instructions tell the victim to run `curl -o /tmp/x https://... && chmod +x /tmp/x && /tmp/x`. Why does Gatekeeper not prompt?
options: Because /tmp is protected by SIP
Because chmod removes the signature
Because Gatekeeper only checks apps from the App Store
Because curl does not set the quarantine attribute, so the launch never invokes Gatekeeper
blocks.explain: Apple's DTS notes that curl does not quarantine downloads. Without the attribute the first-launch assessment is never triggered. The binary still needs a valid (even ad hoc) signature to run on Apple silicon, which attackers can add trivially.

blocks.question: On macOS Sequoia a user wants to open an unnotarized app anyway. What changed compared with earlier versions?
options: It is now impossible to open unnotarized software
The app must be re-signed by IT
Gatekeeper is turned off for admin users
Control-click and Open no longer overrides; the user must approve it in System Settings, Privacy & Security
blocks.explain: Apple's August 2024 note: the Control-click override is gone in Sequoia; the user reviews security information and clicks Open Anyway in System Settings. That extra step is also reported to Endpoint Security clients.

lessons.title: Notarization, revocation and the Shlayer lesson

blocks.md:
**Notarization** is Apple's automated malware scan for software distributed outside the App Store. Apple's [developer documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/notarizing-macos-software-before-distribution) is precise about what it is and is not: "Notarization of macOS software is not App Review. The Apple notary service is an automated system that scans your software for malicious content, checks for code-signing issues, and returns the results to you quickly."

A tiny example: a developer finishes `Notes.app`, signs it with their Developer ID certificate, turns on the hardened runtime, adds a secure timestamp, and uploads it with `notarytool`. Shortly after, the service returns a **ticket**. The developer **staples** it to the app (attaches it to the file) so Gatekeeper can check it even offline; the ticket is also published online.

blocks.title: From upload to revocation

scenes.caption: The developer signs with a Developer ID certificate (hardened runtime and secure timestamp are required) and uploads with notarytool.
No known malware found: the service issues a ticket and publishes it online. The developer staples it to the app.
Gatekeeper sees the ticket at first launch and allows the app after the user confirms.
A researcher reports that a notarized app is malware. Apple revokes the Developer ID certificate and issues revocation tickets.
Macs fetch revocation tickets in the background, more often than XProtect updates, and Gatekeeper now blocks the app even though it was notarized.

blocks.md:
Apple's documentation sets the rules: since macOS 10.15 (Catalina), all software built after 1 June 2019 and distributed with Developer ID must be notarized; the service requires a Developer ID certificate, the hardened runtime (lesson 9) and a secure timestamp. Apple's [malware guide page](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/protecting-against-malware-sec469d47bd8/web) adds the response side: revocation tickets can be issued even for apps that were previously notarized, and "checks for revocation tickets happen in the background much more frequently than even the background updates that push new XProtect signatures".

Notarization also leaves an audit trail: Apple says the notary service records the software distributed with your signing key, so if that key leaks you can ask Apple to revoke the tickets for versions you did not build.

**Case: Shlayer gets notarized (August 2020).** Shlayer is adware that, as TechCrunch summarised, intercepts encrypted web traffic and replaces websites and search results with its own ads; Kaspersky had called it the "most common threat" Macs faced in 2019. On 31 August 2020 [TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2020/08/31/apple-notarized-mac-malware/) that Peter Dantini, working with Mac security researcher Patrick Wardle, had found a malware campaign disguised as an Adobe Flash installer whose payloads were **notarized**. The researchers said it was the first Mac malware inadvertently notarized by Apple ("As far as I know, this is a first," Wardle wrote).

Apple told TechCrunch it "revoked the identified variant, disabled the developer account, and revoked the associated certificates". Wardle reported the attackers were back soon after with a new notarized payload, which Apple also blocked.

Notarization means "Apple's automated scan found nothing known-bad when this was uploaded". It is not a review of intent, and it can be fooled by code that only turns malicious later or hides its payload. Its real strength is speed of revocation once something is reported.

**Defender's view.**

- **Prevent**: keep Gatekeeper at App Store and identified developers, and block overrides through MDM where the business allows.
- **Detect**: `spctl --assess -vv` shows `source=Notarized Developer ID` and the Developer ID name; record the Team ID of every app in your fleet inventory (lesson 13) so a newly seen Team ID stands out.
- **Respond**: when a vendor's Team ID is implicated (as in 3CX, lesson 17), block it with your endpoint tool rather than waiting for Apple's revocation to reach every Mac.

blocks.question: A colleague says "the installer is notarized, so it is safe to approve". What is the most accurate reply?
options: Correct: notarized apps are reviewed by Apple staff
Notarization only means an automated scan found no known malware at upload time; Shlayer was notarized twice in 2020
Notarization only applies to App Store apps
Notarization means the app is sandboxed
blocks.explain: Apple itself says notarization is not App Review. Shlayer's notarized payloads show that scanning for known malicious content misses new or disguised code.

blocks.question: Apple wants to stop a notarized app that turns out to be malicious as fast as possible on every Mac. Which mechanism does its guide say is fastest?
options: A notarization revocation ticket checked in the background
A macOS point release
A new XProtect YARA signature
Removing the app from the App Store
blocks.explain: Apple's malware page says revocation-ticket checks happen in the background much more frequently than XProtect signature updates, so revocation is the quickest block for a known-bad, previously notarized app.

lessons.title: XProtect: Apple's built-in signatures and remediators

blocks.md:
**XProtect** is the antivirus built into macOS. Apple's [guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/protecting-against-malware-sec469d47bd8/web) says it uses **YARA** signatures; YARA's [documentation](https://yara.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) describes YARA as "a tool aimed at (but not limited to) helping malware researchers to identify and classify malware samples" by describing families "based on textual or binary patterns".

XProtect checks for known malicious content when an app is first launched, when an app has been changed in the file system, and when its signatures are updated. Apple checks for signature updates daily, independent of OS updates. When it finds known malware it blocks it, moves it to the Trash and alerts the user. The rules are generic enough to catch variants, which a notarization revocation (one file or hash) cannot.

blocks.code:
% xprotect version
Version: 5342 Installed: 2026-05-09 04:44:25 +0000
% B=/var/protected/xprotect/XProtect.bundle/Contents/Resources
% grep -c '^rule ' $B/XProtect.yara
461
% plutil -extract CFBundleShortVersionString raw /Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle/Contents/Info.plist
5287
% ls /Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.app/Contents/MacOS/ | head -5
XProtect
XProtectRemediatorAdload
XProtectRemediatorBadGacha
XProtectRemediatorBlueTop
XProtectRemediatorBundlore
blocks.caption: Real output, read-only. Since macOS 15 the live, updated bundle is in /var/protected/xprotect; the CoreServices copy (5287 here) is only a fallback. The YARA file is world-readable; the installed date is a staleness check on a fleet.

blocks.md: Here is one of Apple's rules from that file, unchanged except for layout. The strings are hex bytes; the condition says when the rule fires.

blocks.caption: Copied from XProtect.yara on macOS 26.7.1 (meta fields omitted).

blocks.md: Decoding the strings (code below) shows a shell script (`#!` at offset 0) that uses `mktemp`, `tail -c`, `funzip`, `chmod +x` and `nohup`, and also contains a zip header (`PK` followed by bytes 3 and 4). That is the shape of a script carrying a zip archive appended to itself, cutting it out and running it in the background.

blocks.code:
b = [bytes.fromhex(h) for h in
     ["6d6b74656d70", "7461696c202d632022", "66756e7a6970202d22",
      "63686d6f64202b78", "6e6f687570"]]
print([s.decode() for s in b])

def rule_54d6414(data: bytes) -> bool:
    # filesize < 100KB and $a at 0 and (all of ($b*)) and $c1
    return (len(data) < 100 * 1024 and data.startswith(b"#!")
            and all(s in data for s in b) and b"PK\x03\x04" in data)

setup = b"#!/bin/sh\nd=$(mktemp -d)\nchmod +x ./tool\n"
odd   = b"#!/bin/sh\n" + b" ".join(b) + b"\nPK\x03\x04..."
print("ordinary script:", rule_54d6414(setup))
print("all five strings + zip header:", rule_54d6414(odd))
# ['mktemp', 'tail -c "', 'funzip -"', 'chmod +x', 'nohup']
# ordinary script: False
# all five strings + zip header: True
blocks.caption: Real run (Python 3). The rule's condition rewritten as Python on in-memory test strings: no real malware involved.

blocks.title: The rule fires only when every condition holds

scenes.caption: The condition is an AND: a #! at offset 0, all five $b strings, and a zip header, in a file under 100 KB.
An ordinary installer script shares some strings (mktemp, chmod +x) but misses the rest: no match. Specific combinations keep false positives low.
A script with every string and an appended zip matches. One rule covers every variant built from that template, whatever its hash.

blocks.md:
**Beyond signatures.** Apple's guide describes two more engines: a **remediation** engine (the `XProtectRemediator...` programs above, each named after a malware family) that removes infections using updates Apple delivers and keeps checking periodically, and a **behavioural** engine that detects unknown malware by what it does. On macOS 26.4 or later, Apple's [Terminal and script protections](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/terminal-and-script-protections-sece3b202c4b/web) extend XProtect to pasted commands and to every AppleScript execution (lesson 16).

**For defenders**, XProtect is not silent: Endpoint Security clients receive `xp_malware_detected` and `xp_malware_remediated` events, including which signature fired, so your EDR (endpoint detection and response) tool or `eslogger` can centralise them.

blocks.question: A new Shlayer variant is rebuilt with a different hash every hour. Which built-in control is best placed to catch it without Apple seeing each copy?
options: An XProtect YARA rule matching patterns shared by the family
A notarization revocation ticket
SIP
The quarantine attribute
blocks.explain: Revocations and hashes name specific files. A YARA rule describes patterns common to the family, so new builds still match. Apple's guide makes exactly this contrast.

blocks.question: When does XProtect's signature scan run, according to Apple?
options: At an app's first launch, when the app changes on disk, and when signatures update
Continuously on every file read
Only during OS updates
Only when the user runs a manual scan
blocks.explain: Apple lists those three triggers (macOS 10.15 or later). It is not a continuous file scanner, which is one reason third-party EDR still adds value.

lessons.title: SIP and the signed system volume: root is not enough

blocks.md: On a classic Unix system, root can change anything, including the OS itself. macOS deliberately breaks that rule. **System Integrity Protection (SIP)** uses, in Apple's [words](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/system-integrity-protection-secb7ea06b49/web), "kernel permissions to limit writability of critical system files", and applies this policy "to every process running on the system, regardless of whether that process is running sandboxed or with administrative privileges". It is mandatory access control from the prerequisite course: a policy users cannot override. SIP has been on by default since OS X 10.11 (El Capitan). Microsoft's researchers note it is also known as **rootless**, the name still visible in its configuration file.

blocks.code:
% csrutil status
System Integrity Protection status: enabled.
% csrutil authenticated-root status
Authenticated Root status: enabled
% ls -lOd /System /usr /usr/local
drwxr-xr-x@ 10 root  wheel  restricted         320 Sep 24 19:06 /System
drwxr-xr-x@ 11 root  wheel  restricted,hidden  352 Sep 24 19:06 /usr
drwxr-xr-x  10 root  wheel  sunlnk             320 Nov 19 17:10 /usr/local
% ls -lO /System/Library/Sandbox/rootless.conf
-rw-r--r--  1 root  wheel  restricted,compressed 5331 Sep 24 19:06 /System/Library/Sandbox/rootless.conf
blocks.caption: Real output, read-only. The restricted flag marks SIP-protected paths; /usr/local is deliberately left writable for admins and package managers.

blocks.md: SIP can only be turned off from recoveryOS (the separate recovery system you boot into), not from a running macOS, so malware with root cannot simply disable it. A small set of Apple processes need to write protected paths, for example the installer. Microsoft's [Shrootless write-up](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/10/28/microsoft-finds-new-macos-vulnerability-shrootless-that-could-bypass-system-integrity-protection/) lists the entitlements that grant this: `com.apple.rootless.install` bypasses SIP's file system checks, and `com.apple.rootless.install.heritable` passes that power to child processes. Only Apple can sign code with them, which makes those processes prime targets.

blocks.title: Shrootless (CVE-2021-30892): a child that inherited too much

scenes.caption: Setup: malware already has root but SIP still blocks writes to protected paths. It writes /etc/zshenv, a file zsh reads at every start, even non-interactive.
An Apple-signed package with a post-install script is installed. system_installd, which holds the heritable rootless entitlement, runs the script with zsh.
zsh sources /etc/zshenv first. The attacker's commands now run in a process that SIP trusts, and can write protected locations.
Apple's fix in macOS 12.0.1 (25 October 2021): "An inherited permissions issue was addressed with additional restrictions." The trust no longer flows to attacker-controlled shell startup files.

blocks.md:
Jonathan Bar Or of Microsoft is credited in Apple's [macOS Monterey 12.0.1 notes](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT212869). Microsoft also pointed out that the per-user `~/.zshenv` behaves the same way and needs no root, so it is a persistence and privilege trap on its own.

**Defender's view.** Prevent: patch; SIP stays on in every baseline. Detect: alert on writes to `/etc/zshenv` and `~/.zshenv`, and on `csrutil` or recovery-mode SIP changes reported by your MDM (osquery's `sip_config` table, lesson 13). Respond: a confirmed SIP bypass means the OS itself may be modified; reinstall rather than clean.

**The signed system volume (SSV).** Since macOS 11 the OS lives on a read-only volume protected cryptographically. Apple's [SSV page](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/signed-system-volume-security-secd698747c9/web) explains: every file's data is hashed with SHA-256, the hashes sit in the file system's metadata tree, which is itself hashed like a Merkle tree (a tree where each parent stores the hash of its children), so the root hash, the **seal**, covers every byte. Apple signs the seal. On Apple silicon the bootloader verifies it before starting the kernel, and data that fails its hash on read is never returned.

blocks.title: The seal: one hash that covers every byte

scenes.caption: Each block of file data is hashed; the hashes live in metadata nodes, which are hashed again up to a single seal that Apple signs.
Someone changes launchd's bytes on disk while the Mac is off. Its hash no longer matches what node A recorded.

If the attacker also rewrites the hashes above it, the seal no longer verifies at boot: startup halts and the user is prompted to reinstall. If not, the data fails its hash when read and is never returned.

blocks.md: Newer macOS versions move some OS parts into **cryptexes**, sealed disk images that Apple can patch between full updates (Background Security Improvements, macOS 26.1 or later). That is why `/Applications/Safari.app` on a current Mac is a symlink into `/System/Cryptexes/App/...`.

blocks.question: Malware gains root on a Mac with SIP enabled and tries to replace `/usr/bin/sudo`. What happens?
options: It succeeds, because root can write anywhere
It succeeds only if the Mac has no FileVault
macOS asks the user for permission
The write is denied: SIP applies to every process, including root
blocks.explain: Apple's SIP page: the policy applies regardless of administrative privileges. /usr is also on the read-only signed system volume. Root malware has to go through an entitled Apple process or a bug, as Shrootless did.

blocks.question: Why did Shrootless need an Apple-signed package?
options: Apple packages are not scanned by XProtect
Apple packages disable Gatekeeper
Its installer daemon holds a heritable entitlement that lets child processes bypass SIP, and the post-install script ran as such a child
zsh is only used by Apple packages
blocks.explain: The SIP bypass was borrowed trust: system_installd's heritable rootless entitlement flowed to the zsh child, and zsh read the attacker's /etc/zshenv. Apple's fix restricted what is inherited.

lessons.title: TCC: consent prompts, the databases and who is asking

blocks.md:
You have seen the dialog: "Zoom would like to access the camera". Behind it is **TCC**, Transparency, Consent, and Control; Apple's [guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/controlling-app-access-to-files-secddd1d86a6/web) states the goal as users having "full transparency, consent, and control over what apps are doing with their data". Microsoft's researchers date it to OS X Mountain Lion in 2012.

TCC is a second permission system on top of Unix file permissions. Your shell can read `~/Documents` by Unix rules, yet a new app running as you is stopped until you consent. That is the point: malware running as the user should not get the user's private data for free.

**What TCC guards on macOS**, per Apple: Calendars, Camera, Contacts, Microphone, Photos, Reminders, Speech recognition, Input Monitoring (keystrokes), Screen Recording, and System Settings; files in Desktop, Documents, Downloads, iCloud Drive, network and removable volumes (macOS 10.15 or later); Full Disk Access (access to the whole storage device); and Accessibility and Automation (Apple events, one app scripting another), which, Apple notes, "require user permission to help ensure that they don't circumvent other protections".

Some of these the user approves at a prompt; for others (Accessibility, Full Disk Access) the user has to go into System Settings, Privacy & Security, and switch the app on.

blocks.title: First request, prompt, and remembered answer

scenes.caption: Zoom asks for the camera. The request goes to tccd, the TCC daemon (one runs per user, one as root).
tccd looks for a stored decision for this app's code identity and this service. None exists yet.
So the user is prompted. Their answer is written to the database with the app's code requirement (csreq).
Next time the record answers without a prompt, but only for code that still satisfies the stored requirement. A different binary claiming the same name does not match.

blocks.md:
Microsoft's [powerdir write-up](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/01/10/new-macos-vulnerability-powerdir-could-lead-to-unauthorized-user-data-access/) describes the storage: a **user database** at `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db` and a **system database** at `/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db`, both SQLite. Camera and microphone access sit in the user database; Full Disk Access and Screen Capture in the system one. The system database is protected by SIP, and reading either requires Full Disk Access. (We do not open them in this course: doing so needs Full Disk Access, which is exactly the point.)

The `csreq` column holds the app's **designated requirement**, the rule from its code signature that says which future code counts as "the same app":

blocks.code:
% codesign -d -r- "/Applications/Google Chrome.app" | tail -1
designated => (identifier "com.google.Chrome" or identifier "com.google.Chrome.beta" or
  identifier "com.google.Chrome.dev" or identifier "com.google.Chrome.canary") and anchor apple
  generic and certificate 1[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.6] /* exists */ and certificate
  leaf[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.1.13] /* exists */ and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = EQHXZ8M8AV
% codesign -d -r- Toy.app | tail -1
# designated => cdhash H"8d668a6cea815a22e53ee19af9cb9c5fc2bc2bbf"
blocks.caption: Real output (line breaks added). Chrome's requirement names the bundle IDs, an Apple-issued Developer ID chain and Team ID EQHXZ8M8AV, so updates keep their grants. The ad hoc toy is pinned to one cdhash.

blocks.md:
**The responsible process.** TCC attributes a request to the app *responsible* for it, not only to the process that made the system call. The `eslogger` manual shows why that matters: run from Terminal, `eslogger` works only if Terminal itself has Full Disk Access. Everything launched from a terminal that holds Full Disk Access inherits that reach, which is why attackers aim to get a terminal, or a user, to grant it.

**Fleet control.** On managed Macs, the Privacy Preferences Policy Control (PPPC) payload (`com.apple.TCC.configuration-profile-policy`) pre-approves services per app. Apple's [payload reference](https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/privacy-preferences-policy-control-payload-dep38df53c2a/web) lets MDM allow Full Disk Access or Accessibility, but for Camera, Microphone and Screen Recording only to **deny**: those stay the user's decision.

Granting Full Disk Access to Terminal, an IDE or a remote-management agent is common, and it means anything running under that app can read Mail, Messages and every TCC-protected folder. Inventory which apps hold Full Disk Access across the fleet, and treat a new grant as an event worth reviewing (Endpoint Security reports `tcc_modify`).

blocks.question: Malware running as the user tries to read `~/Documents/contracts.pdf`. Unix permissions allow it. What decides the outcome?
options: TCC: the malware's process needs the user's consent (or Full Disk Access) for Documents
Nothing: Unix permissions are final
SIP, because Documents is a system folder
Gatekeeper, because the file was downloaded
blocks.explain: Documents is TCC-protected on macOS 10.15 or later. The responsible app needs a stored allow for Documents or Full Disk Access; otherwise tccd denies or prompts.

blocks.question: An MDM admin wants Zoom to use the camera without a prompt on every laptop. What does Apple's PPPC payload allow?
options: Only deny camera access; allowing it stays the user's choice
Allow camera for Zoom silently
Disable TCC for Zoom
Grant Full Disk Access instead
blocks.explain: Apple's PPPC reference: Camera, Microphone and Screen Recording settings can only deny. The user still approves the prompt the first time.

lessons.title: Breaking TCC: $HOME poisoning, powerdir and XCSSET

blocks.md: A TCC bypass is any way for code to reach protected data or abilities without the consent the user would have been asked for. They are a well-studied bug class: MITRE tracks the technique as [T1548.006 TCC Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/006/). Three fixed bugs show the three classic angles: trick tccd into reading the wrong database, plant a database in a home directory you control, or borrow another app's permissions. We look at each mechanism next to Apple's fix, without exploit steps.

**1. CVE-2020-9934: trusting `$HOME`.** As Microsoft summarises it, the user's tccd built the path to its database by expanding `$HOME/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db`. `$HOME` is just an environment variable, and a user could change the one launchd passes to tccd. Point it at a folder you control, put your own TCC.db there with "allow" rows, and tccd would read your answers. Apple fixed it in [macOS Catalina 10.15.6](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT211289) (15 July 2020), crediting Matt Shockley: "An issue existed in the handling of environment variables." Microsoft read the fix: tccd now asks for the home directory with `getpwuid()` on the real user ID. The bug and the fix fit in a few lines of Python:

blocks.code:
import os, pwd

SUFFIX = "Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db"

def db_path_vulnerable():
    # trusts an environment variable the caller controls
    return os.path.join(os.environ["HOME"], SUFFIX)

def db_path_fixed():
    # asks the user database for this uid's home directory
    return os.path.join(pwd.getpwuid(os.getuid()).pw_dir, SUFFIX)

fake = "/tmp/fakehome"
print("vulnerable:", db_path_vulnerable())
print("fixed uses fake home?", db_path_fixed().startswith(fake))

# $ HOME=/tmp/fakehome python3 tcc_path.py
# vulnerable: /tmp/fakehome/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db
# fixed uses fake home? False
blocks.caption: Real run: a model of the path logic only, not tccd's code. The fix stops trusting the caller's environment.

blocks.md: **2. CVE-2021-30970 "powerdir": change the home directory itself.** Jonathan Bar Or of Microsoft asked whether the fix went deep enough: `getpwuid()` returns the home directory stored in the user's directory record, so what if that record changes? Changing it with `dscl` (the Directory Services command-line tool) needed a TCC permission, but Microsoft found that exporting the user's record with `dsexport`, editing it and importing it with `dsimport` avoided that check, and tccd would then load a planted database from the new home. Apple fixed it in [macOS Monterey 12.1](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT212978) (13 December 2021): "A logic issue was addressed with improved state management."

**3. CVE-2021-30713, used by XCSSET: borrow a donor app.** Researchers at [Jamf](https://www.jamf.com/blog/zero-day-tcc-bypass-discovered-in-xcsset-malware/), a company that sells Apple device management and security software (Jamf Protect), found the XCSSET malware, which spread through infected Xcode projects, searching for installed apps that users commonly allow to record the screen (Zoom among them), then placing its own small ad hoc signed AppleScript app *inside* that app's bundle. TCC decided whose permissions applied from the bundle, so the nested app inherited the donor's Screen Recording grant. Apple fixed it in [macOS Big Sur 11.4](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT212529) (24 May 2021), noting it "may have been actively exploited".

blocks.title: XCSSET's donor-app trick (fixed in macOS 11.4)

scenes.caption: The user once allowed Zoom to record the screen. That decision is stored for Zoom's code identity.
The malware compiles a tiny AppleScript app and places it inside Zoom's bundle, signing it ad hoc.
When the nested app takes a screenshot, the vulnerable logic attributed it to the enclosing bundle and found Zoom's grant: no prompt.
The fix validates the code that is actually asking. Jamf's detection idea still works for hunting: an app inside another app's bundle whose signer differs from the parent.

blocks.md:
**Defender's view across all three.**

- **Prevent**: patch promptly; TCC bugs are fixed in point releases, and Apple noted CVE-2021-30713 may have been actively exploited before its fix.
- **Detect**: Endpoint Security reports `tcc_modify` (permission changes) and Open Directory events such as `od_attribute_set` (changes to user records, the powerdir angle); alert on unexpected `dsimport`, on a `TCC.db` file written outside the two real locations, and on a nested `.app` whose Team ID differs from its parent bundle.
- **Respond**: list the apps holding Screen Recording, Accessibility and Full Disk Access on the affected Mac, compare against your PPPC baseline, and revoke grants nobody can explain.

All three bugs answer the same question wrongly: *who is asking, and where are their rules?* Fixes moved from trusting caller-controlled inputs ($HOME, the directory record, the bundle path) to checking the code that is actually running.

blocks.question: Apple's fix for CVE-2020-9934 replaced `$HOME` with `getpwuid()`. Why was that not the end of the story?
options: getpwuid() is slower
getpwuid() does not work as root
It still trusted the user's directory record, and powerdir found a way to change that record's home directory
It removed the user database
blocks.explain: The fix removed one attacker-controlled input (an environment variable) but kept a dependency on the stored home directory. Microsoft changed that via dsexport/dsimport, leading to CVE-2021-30970.

blocks.question: Which hunting query best matches the XCSSET technique?
options: Apps signed with a Developer ID
Any AppleScript file
An application bundle found inside another application's bundle with a different signer
Apps with the quarantine attribute
blocks.explain: Jamf's detection checks for an app bundled within another app and compares their signatures. Legitimate helpers inside a bundle are signed by the same team.

lessons.title: Hardened runtime, library validation and dylib injection

blocks.md:
Code signing proves a file is unchanged on disk. It says nothing about what gets *added* to the process at run time. On macOS, the dynamic linker `dyld` loads shared libraries (`.dylib`) into every program, and it historically honoured environment variables such as `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, which loads an extra library into the process before `main()`. MITRE tracks this abuse as T1574.006 (Dynamic Linker Hijacking).

Here is the problem made concrete on our own toy binary. The extra library only prints a line.

blocks.title: One binary, two signatures, one environment variable
blocks.code:
#include <stdio.h>  /* extra.c: constructor runs at load */
__attribute__((constructor)) static void init(void) {
    puts("extra.dylib constructor ran"); }

% clang -dynamiclib -o extra.dylib extra.c
% DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES=./extra.dylib ./hello
extra.dylib constructor ran
hello from a toy app
% cp hello hello-hr
% codesign -f -s - -o runtime hello-hr
hello-hr: replacing existing signature
% DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES=./extra.dylib ./hello-hr
hello from a toy app

scenes.caption: A tiny library with a constructor: code that runs as soon as the library is loaded, before the program's main().
Plain ad hoc signed binary: dyld honours DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES, so foreign code runs inside the process with all of its permissions (including any TCC grants).
scenes.output:
extra.dylib constructor ran
hello from a toy app

scenes.caption: Re-sign the same binary with the hardened runtime option (-o runtime).
Now dyld ignores the variable. Same code, same environment, but the injected constructor never runs. Real output from this course's lab.

blocks.md:
The **hardened runtime** is an opt-in set of protections chosen at signing time. Apple's [documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/hardened-runtime) says it protects "the runtime integrity of your software by preventing certain classes of exploits, like code injection, dynamically linked library (DLL) hijacking, and process memory space tampering". `codesign`'s manual lists what `runtime` turns on: "runtime code signing enforcement, library validation, hard, kill, and debugging restrictions".

**Library validation** means the process may only load system libraries or libraries signed with the same Team ID as the main executable, so an attacker's dylib dropped next to the app is refused. Notarization requires the hardened runtime, so apps notarized under the current rules have it (Apple relaxes some rules for preexisting software).

blocks.code:
% codesign -dvv "/Applications/Google Chrome.app" 2>&1 | grep flags
CodeDirectory v=20500 size=765 flags=0x12a00(kill,restrict,library-validation,runtime) ...
% codesign -d --entitlements - --xml "/Applications/Google Chrome.app" | plutil -p - | grep -c 'security\.cs\.'
0
blocks.caption: Real output. Chrome runs with the hardened runtime and library validation and requests none of the com.apple.security.cs exception entitlements.

blocks.md:
**Where the sandbox fits.** The prerequisite course showed the App Sandbox: entitlements that confine an app to its own container. The hardened runtime is different: it protects the process *from others* (injection, debugging, tampering), while the sandbox limits what the process itself may reach. Mac App Store apps must be sandboxed. The sandbox is driven by profiles: Apple's own daemons ship hundreds of them in `/System/Library/Sandbox/Profiles`, and `sandbox-exec`, the old command-line way to apply a custom profile, is marked DEPRECATED in its manual. Developer ID apps must be hardened to be notarized, but the sandbox is optional for them, so outside the App Store TCC is often the only thing between an app and your files.

**Limits.** Library validation compares Team IDs. If the attacker controls the vendor's build and signing (3CX, lesson 17), the malicious library carries the right Team ID and loads normally.

A quick fleet hunt: list apps whose entitlements contain `allow-dyld-environment-variables` or `disable-library-validation`, then check which of them also hold TCC grants. osquery's `signature` table exposes an `entitlements` column for exactly this (lesson 13).

blocks.question: An attacker sets `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` in a LaunchAgent that starts a notarized app which holds Full Disk Access. Assuming no exception entitlements, what happens?
options: The library loads and inherits Full Disk Access
Gatekeeper blocks the LaunchAgent
SIP deletes the library
dyld ignores the variable because notarized apps run with the hardened runtime
blocks.explain: Notarization requires the hardened runtime, under which DYLD environment variables are ignored unless the app has the allow-dyld-environment-variables entitlement. That is exactly why that entitlement is worth inventorying.

blocks.question: What does library validation compare when deciding whether a dylib may load?
options: The dylib's file name
Whether the dylib is notarized
Whether the dylib is a platform library or signed with the same Team ID as the main executable
The dylib's size
blocks.explain: Per the codesign manual and Apple's signing guide: system libraries, or libraries carrying the same team identifier. A library signed by another developer, or ad hoc, is refused.

lessons.title: Persistence on macOS: launchd, login items and BTM

blocks.code:
% plutil -p fixtures/LaunchAgents/com.example.backup.plist
{
  "Label" => "com.example.backup"
  "ProgramArguments" => [
    0 => "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome"
    1 => "--version"
  ]
  "StartInterval" => 3600
}
% plutil -lint fixtures/LaunchAgents/*.plist
fixtures/LaunchAgents/com.apple.updater.plist: OK
fixtures/LaunchAgents/com.example.backup.plist: OK
blocks.caption: Real output on two plists written to a scratch fixtures folder. They were never loaded with launchctl.

blocks.md:
The keys that matter when triaging, from `man launchd.plist`:

- `Label`: required, "uniquely identifies the job". Attackers pick names like `com.apple.*` or `com.google.keystone.*` to blend in.
- `Program` / `ProgramArguments`: what runs. The first thing to check: where is that file, and who signed it?
- `RunAtLoad`: start when loaded (at login for agents). The manual says it "should be avoided", so it is mildly suspicious alone.
- `KeepAlive`: restart it whenever it exits.
- `StartInterval`, `WatchPaths`: run on a timer or when a path changes.

blocks.title: What runs at login, and where defenders look

scenes.caption: launchd loads jobs from three writable folders. The user folder needs no admin rights at all, which is why commodity stealers favour it.
Since macOS 13, Background Task Management tracks login items, launch agents and launch daemons as they are added.
The user gets a notification and sees the item under System Settings, General, Login Items; managed Macs can pre-approve known items by Team ID.
Security tools receive btm_launch_item_add from Endpoint Security, so a new agent is an event, not something found weeks later.

blocks.md: **Background Task Management (BTM).** Apple's [deployment guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/manage-login-items-background-tasks-mac-depdca572563/web) explains that from macOS 13 a framework "is used to create transparency to the user when you configure login items, launch agents, and launch daemons". Admins can pre-approve items with a Managed Login Items payload, matching by bundle ID, Team ID or launchd `Label`. `sfltool dumpbtm` prints every registered item (it asks for an administrator password, so it is not run here), and the log subsystem `com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagement` records changes. ATT&CK [T1547.015](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/015/) covers login items.

**Real examples.** Microsoft's May 2026 analysis of macOS ClickFix campaigns (fake fix instructions that get users to paste a command into Terminal themselves; lesson 16) found stealers writing a LaunchAgent named `com.google.keystone.agent.plist` (a name imitating Google's updater), random `com.<value>.plist` agents, and `/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.finder.helper.plist`. Mandiant, the incident response and threat intelligence firm now part of Google Cloud, found the attackers behind 3CX kept their backdoor on 3CX's macOS build server using Launch Daemons.

blocks.caption: Real run on the fixtures: a fake com.apple.updater pointing at an ad hoc binary in a hidden folder, and a benign job. Point it at a copy of real folders during an investigation.

blocks.md: Look beyond launchd: Microsoft's Shrootless research showed `~/.zshenv` runs for every zsh, including under `sudo`. Shell startup files, login items and browser extensions are all persistence. A new agent is cheap for the attacker; your job is to make it loud.

blocks.question: A stealer has no admin password. Which persistence location is it most likely to use?
options: ~/Library/LaunchAgents
/Library/LaunchDaemons
/System/Library/LaunchAgents
/usr/libexec
blocks.explain: The per-user LaunchAgents folder is writable by the user. /Library needs admin rights, and /System and /usr are on the sealed, SIP-protected system volume.

blocks.question: A plist in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` has Label `com.apple.softwareupdate.helper` and runs `/Users/Shared/.svc/helper`, signed ad hoc. Which finding is the strongest single signal?
options: An Apple-looking label whose program is not Apple-signed and lives in a hidden shared folder
RunAtLoad is set
The file is a binary plist
The job has a Label
blocks.explain: Apple's own agents live on the system volume and are Apple-signed. A com.apple label on an ad hoc binary in a hidden folder is masquerading, the pattern Microsoft documented with com.google.keystone.

lessons.title: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded

blocks.md:
On Linux you learned to read text logs in `/var/log` and the journal. macOS replaced most of that with the **unified logging system**. Apple's [logging documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/os/logging) says it is available from macOS 10.12, "supersedes the Apple System Logger (ASL) and Syslog APIs", and "centralizes the storage of log data in memory and on disk, rather than writing that data to a text-based log file". You read it with the Console app or the `log` command-line tool.

Each message carries a **subsystem** (usually a reverse-DNS name like `com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagement`), a **category**, a process, and a **level**: debug, info, default, error or fault. Debug and info messages are by default kept only in memory, so collect early.
Here is the whole loop on our own program: write three messages with `os_log`, then query them. Note the `%{public}s` modifier.

blocks.caption: Real run. Df is a default-level message, E an error. In zsh, log is a shell builtin, so call /usr/bin/log.

blocks.md: The second line says `<private>`. Apple's documentation explains the rule: by default the system "doesn't redact integer, floating-point and Boolean values, but it does redact the contents of dynamic strings and complex dynamic objects". Developers opt values in with `%{public}`. For investigators this is the biggest surprise in Mac logs: user names, paths and URLs are often missing from the very lines you need. Endpoint Security (next lesson) fills that gap.

blocks.title: From os_log call to the analyst's query

scenes.caption: A process logs a message tagged with subsystem, category and level.
Lower levels live in memory and roll over quickly; default and above are written to the on-disk store. Simplified: retention varies with volume and settings.
Analysts filter with predicates (subsystem, process, eventMessage CONTAINS ...). osquery exposes the same data as a table.
For incident response, log collect writes a .logarchive you can copy off the Mac and query later with log show --archive.

blocks.md:
**Predicates worth knowing.** Apple's deployment guide itself suggests `subsystem == "com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagement"` for login item changes. Endpoint Security events can be written into the log with `eslogger --oslog` (default subsystem `com.apple.eslogger`), which turns the log into a basic EDR feed on a lab Mac.

**Evidence handling.** `log collect --output case.logarchive` (needs admin) captures the store into one bundle for the timeline. The `log` tool also has an `erase` command; attackers clearing logs is ATT&CK T1685.006 (Clear Linux or Mac System Logs, formerly T1070.002), so ship logs off the Mac and alert on gaps.

Do not expect an attacker's password prompt, curl URL or file path to show up in plain text in the unified log. Default privacy redaction hides many dynamic strings. Plan on Endpoint Security or EDR telemetry for process command lines, and use the unified log for subsystem state changes.

blocks.question: Your query returns `opened <private>` where you hoped to see a file path. Why?
options: The log was tampered with
The path was too long
Dynamic strings are redacted by default unless the developer marked them public
The message was at debug level
blocks.explain: Apple's documentation: the unified log redacts dynamic strings and objects by default; developers opt in with %{public}. Integers and Booleans are not redacted.

blocks.question: You are called to a Mac two days after suspicious activity. Which log data is most likely gone already?
options: Info and debug messages, which are kept in memory by default
Fault messages
Error messages
All messages older than one hour
blocks.explain: Debug and info messages are by default not persisted, so they roll over quickly. Default, error and fault messages reach the persistent store, which is why log collect early matters.

lessons.title: Endpoint Security: the API every Mac EDR is built on

blocks.md:
Every serious Mac security product (EDR, application allowlisting, data loss prevention) is now built on one Apple API. Apple's [documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/endpointsecurity) describes **Endpoint Security (ES)** as "a C API for monitoring system events for potentially malicious activity", used from a **system extension** (code that runs in user space but is installed and protected by the OS). Clients either **authorize** pending events or receive **notifications** of events that already happened.

It replaced kernel extensions (kexts). Apple's [kernel page](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/securely-extending-the-kernel-sec8e454101b/web) is blunt: "Kexts are no longer recommended for macOS", and on Apple silicon loading one requires booting to recovery and lowering the Mac to Reduced Security. Security agents should use ES instead. On Windows, EDR sensors rely on kernel callbacks; ES is the Mac equivalent.

blocks.title: An AUTH event: an allowlisting tool decides whether a binary may run

scenes.caption: The user runs a program. The kernel pauses the exec and sends ES_EVENT_TYPE_AUTH_EXEC to every subscribed client.
The client reads the event: path, cdhash, signing ID, Team ID, parent process. It checks its rules.
Lockdown policy: deny. The kernel refuses the exec; the client's own app can tell the user why. A NOTIFY client would only have recorded it.
Every AUTH message has a deadline. Miss it and, per Apple's header, the client is killed by default, so clients must answer fast and can cache results.

blocks.md:
**AUTH vs NOTIFY.** AUTH events (`ES_EVENT_TYPE_AUTH_EXEC`, `AUTH_OPEN`, ...) pause the operation until the client answers allow or deny; NOTIFY events report what happened. The SDK header documents a per-message `deadline`: "If a client fails to respond to auth events prior to the deadline, the client will be killed." Results can be cached, and "a cache hit leads to no AUTH event being produced". To create a client at all, the app needs the `com.apple.developer.endpoint-security.client` entitlement, which developers must request from Apple, and users or MDM must approve the extension and grant Full Disk Access.

**What it sees.** Apple ships `eslogger`, which prints ES notify events as JSON. Its manual says it must run as root with Full Disk Access for the responsible process and supports no AUTH events. Listing the event names needs neither:

blocks.code:
% eslogger --list-events | wc -l
     104
% eslogger --list-events | grep -E '^(exec|gatekeeper|xp_|btm|tcc|login|sudo|su$|od_create_user|profile|screensharing)'
btm_launch_item_add
btm_launch_item_remove
exec
gatekeeper_user_override
login_login
login_logout
od_create_user
profile_add
profile_remove
screensharing_attach
screensharing_detach
su
sudo
tcc_modify
xp_malware_detected
xp_malware_remediated
blocks.caption: Real output on macOS 26.7.1. Capturing events (sudo eslogger exec ...) needs root and Full Disk Access, so it is not run here.

blocks.md:
Those names map straight onto this course: `exec` gives full command lines and the parent process; `gatekeeper_user_override` (lesson 3); `xp_malware_detected` (lesson 5); `tcc_modify` and `od_*` events (lesson 8); `btm_launch_item_add` (lesson 10); `profile_add` (lesson 14). The `eslogger` manual also warns its JSON "is NOT API" and may change, so production tools use the C API.

**Santa**, a binary and file access authorization system originally from Google and now maintained by North Pole Security ([northpolesec/santa](https://github.com/northpolesec/santa); Google's repository says it stopped maintaining Santa in 2025), is a good example of an AUTH client (its README says it is named Santa because it keeps track of binaries that are naughty or nice). In MONITOR mode it allows everything not explicitly blocked and logs every launch; in LOCKDOWN mode only allowlisted binaries run. Rules can match a binary's SHA-256 hash, a CDHash, a certificate, a Team ID or a signing ID.

Endpoint Security is to a Mac what kernel callbacks plus ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) are to Windows: the one place a security product can see every exec, file open, login and permission change, and block some of them. When choosing a Mac EDR, ask which ES events it subscribes to and which it uses in AUTH mode.

blocks.question: A vendor wants to block unknown binaries before they run. Which ES design fits?
options: Subscribe to NOTIFY_EXEC and kill the process afterwards
Use eslogger with --oslog
Load a kernel extension
Subscribe to AUTH_EXEC and answer allow or deny within the deadline
blocks.explain: Only AUTH events pause the operation for a decision. NOTIFY arrives after the fact; eslogger supports no AUTH events; kexts are deprecated and need Reduced Security on Apple silicon.

blocks.question: An ES client takes too long to answer an AUTH_EXEC event. What does Apple's header say happens by default?
options: The exec is denied
The client is killed
The event is retried
Nothing; the exec waits forever
blocks.explain: The deadline field documentation: a client that fails to respond before the deadline is killed (the default deadline-miss mode). That is why clients cache results and keep AUTH handlers fast.

lessons.title: Hunting across a fleet: osquery tables and detection logic

blocks.md:
Two detections from earlier lessons, written as SQL. osquery is not installed on the Mac used to write this course, so they were run in `sqlite3` against stand-in tables with the same column names and toy rows (paths and names invented, patterned on Microsoft's 2026 report). In osquery the same queries run against live data.

The first finds persistence whose program has no Developer ID identity. The second finds a password check (`dscl . -authonly`, which Microsoft observed stealers using to validate a stolen password) and shows who launched it.

blocks.code:
-- 1. launchd jobs whose program is unsigned or has no Team ID
SELECT l.label, s.signed, s.team_identifier AS team
FROM launchd l
JOIN signature s ON s.path = COALESCE(NULLIF(l.program,''),
     substr(l.program_arguments, 1, instr(l.program_arguments || ' ', ' ') - 1))
WHERE l.path NOT LIKE '/System/%' AND l.path NOT LIKE '/Library/Apple/%'
  AND (s.signed = 0 OR s.team_identifier = '');

label                      signed  team
-------------------------  ------  ----
com.google.keystone.agent  1
com.finder.helper          0

-- 2. dscl -authonly with parent and grandparent
SELECT c.pid, p.path AS parent, g.path AS grandparent, c.cmdline
FROM es_process_events c
LEFT JOIN es_process_events p ON p.pid = c.parent
LEFT JOIN es_process_events g ON g.pid = p.parent
WHERE c.path = '/usr/bin/dscl' AND c.cmdline LIKE '%-authonly%';

pid  parent   grandparent         cmdline
---  -------  ------------------  -------------------------
510  /bin/sh  /usr/bin/osascript  dscl . -authonly ana ****
blocks.caption: Real sqlite3 output on toy rows. Apple's own jobs are filtered out by path, because Apple platform binaries have no Team ID either. The real Google updater is signed with Google's Team ID; a keystone label with an empty Team ID is the masquerade from lesson 10.

blocks.title: Which data source sees which technique (simplified)

scenes.caption: 1 means the source records that step directly. Simplified model: real coverage depends on configuration, and exec only shows a command line, not intent.
Process execution events (with full command lines and parents) cover the most steps of a stealer: curl, osascript, dscl, security, zip.
Persistence shows up three ways: the exec that wrote it, the BTM event when it registers, and osquery's launchd table on the next scan.
Some steps have exactly one witness: a TCC permission change only appears as tcc_modify. Lose that event source and the step is invisible.

blocks.md:
**Detection ideas that come straight from public reports** (each one is a starting point to tune against your own baseline, not a finished rule):

- Terminal or a shell whose ancestry starts at a browser or chat app, followed within seconds by `curl` and `osascript` or `bash` (Microsoft's ClickFix guidance: "flag unusual sequences of macOS utilities (curl, Base64, Gunzip, osascript, and dscl)").
- `dscl . -authonly` run by anything other than your admin tooling.
- New `launchd` jobs or BTM items whose program has no Team ID, or a `com.apple.*` label on a non-Apple binary.
- A nested `.app` whose Team ID differs from its parent bundle (XCSSET, lesson 8).
- Any `gatekeeper_user_override` or `tcc_modify` granting Full Disk Access, Accessibility or Screen Recording.
- A Team ID from a vendor advisory (3CX's was `33CF4654HL`, lesson 17) appearing in `signature`.

Mac fleets are full of developers who run curl, shells and unsigned tools all day. Rules that fire on "osascript ran" drown a SOC. Anchor detections on combinations and ancestry (browser to Terminal to curl to osascript to dscl) and on things legitimate tools rarely do (validating a user's password from a script).

blocks.question: Your EDR shows `/usr/bin/dscl . -authonly ana` whose grandparent is `osascript`, launched from Terminal two seconds after a paste. What is the best reading?
options: Routine directory lookup
Likely a script validating a password the user just typed into a fake prompt: escalate
A macOS update
Harmless because dscl is Apple-signed
blocks.explain: Microsoft observed stealers validating captured passwords with dscl -authonly. Apple-signed tools used in an attacker's sequence are living-off-the-land (abusing tools already on the system); the ancestry is what makes it suspicious.

blocks.question: Which osquery table would you join to `launchd` to find persistence items without a Developer ID?
options: sip_config
unified_log
gatekeeper
signature
blocks.explain: signature returns signed, identifier, team_identifier and authority for a path, so joining on the job's program shows who, if anyone, signed it.

lessons.title: Managing a Mac fleet: MDM, profiles and declarative management

blocks.md:
Everything so far was one Mac. Companies run thousands, and the controls only help if they are on, configured the same way and provably so. That is **device management**. Apple's [introduction](https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/intro-to-device-management-depc0aadd3fe/web) describes a device management service as one that lets IT "securely and remotely configure devices by sending configurations, profiles, and commands", including updating software, monitoring compliance, and remotely wiping or locking devices. It is usually called **MDM** (mobile device management), for Macs as well as phones.

A tiny example: a new laptop is shipped straight to an employee. When they turn it on and connect to Wi-Fi, it already knows it belongs to the company, enrols itself, turns on FileVault, installs the EDR system extension and approves it, and the employee never sees an admin password.

blocks.title: Zero-touch setup with Automated Device Enrollment

scenes.caption: The organisation bought the Mac; its serial number is assigned to the company's MDM server in Apple Business (or Apple School Manager).
At first boot Setup Assistant asks Apple whether this device belongs to an organisation and gets the MDM enrollment details.
The Mac enrols. MDM can hold it in Setup Assistant until critical configuration is applied, and can prevent the user removing management later.
Optionally the user signs in at the company identity provider (IdP, the single sign-on service); Platform SSO can create the local account from it.
From now on the Mac reports status and receives new policy. Removing management is blocked for supervised Macs.

blocks.md: **Enrollment matters for security.** Apple's [Automated Device Enrollment page](https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/automated-device-enrollment-management-dep73069dd57/web) lists options only organisation-owned, supervised devices get: *Prevent unenrollment* ("this prevents unenrollment from System Settings as well as from the profiles command-line tool"), *Hold device in Setup Assistant* until critical configuration or apps are installed, a minimum OS version enforced during enrollment (macOS 14 or later), and *Enforce FileVault* during setup with the recovery key escrowed to the service. A user-enrolled personal Mac gets far less control, by design.

**Configuration profiles** are signed plists of **payloads**, each managing one area. The ones a security team touches most:

- **Privacy Preferences Policy Control** (lesson 7): pre-approve TCC services for the EDR and IT agents.
- **System Extensions**: allow the EDR's Endpoint Security extension by Team ID so users are not asked.
- **Managed Login Items** (lesson 10): pre-approve your own agents so new unknown items stand out.
- **FileVault**, **Firewall**, **Software Update** and restrictions such as disallowing the Gatekeeper override.

blocks.code:
% profiles status -type enrollment
Enrolled via DEP: No
MDM enrollment: No
blocks.caption: Real output on this course's lab Mac, a personal unmanaged machine. On an organisation-owned Mac enrolled automatically you would expect Yes for both ("DEP" in the output refers to that automated enrollment). An attacker removing a profile is reported to Endpoint Security as profile_remove.

blocks.md:
**Declarative device management (DDM).** Classic MDM is command and poll: the server sends a command, asks again later whether it worked. Apple's [DDM introduction](https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/intro-to-declarative-device-management-depb1bab77f8/web) describes the newer model: "you define the target configuration state of a device and the device autonomically attempts to achieve and maintain that state", and status reports reach the server proactively "without having to poll the device". For security that means faster drift detection: if FileVault or a required OS version falls out of policy, the device reports it.

DDM also carries software update enforcement: deadlines, deferrals and minimum versions. Patch speed is the control behind every CVE in this course.

Do not build baselines from scratch. The macOS Security Compliance Project (mSCP), run by NIST with other US agencies, generates configuration profiles, DDM declarations, documentation and compliance-check scripts from a chosen benchmark, with rules mapped to NIST SP 800-53 (lesson 18).

blocks.question: A user on a supervised, Automated-Device-Enrolled Mac runs `sudo profiles remove` on the MDM enrollment profile. What does Apple's documentation say happens?
options: Removal is prevented, both from System Settings and from the profiles tool
It succeeds, since the user is an admin
The Mac is wiped
Only FileVault is turned off
blocks.explain: Prevent unenrollment applies to supervised devices and blocks removal from System Settings and from the profiles command-line tool. That is why organisation-owned Macs should use Automated Device Enrollment.

blocks.question: What is the main difference between declarative device management and classic MDM commands?
options: DDM works only on iPhone
DDM does not need enrollment
DDM sends a desired state that the device maintains and reports on proactively, instead of the server issuing commands and polling
DDM replaces FileVault
blocks.explain: Apple's DDM introduction: the device autonomically achieves and maintains the declared state and reports status changes without the server polling.

lessons.title: FileVault, secure boot and startup security

blocks.md:
A stolen laptop is the oldest Mac incident there is. Two controls decide whether the thief gets data or just hardware: **FileVault** encryption, and the **secure boot** chain that stops a modified OS from asking for the password.

Apple's [FileVault page](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/volume-encryption-with-filevault-sec4c6dc1b6e/web) gives the mechanism. FileVault uses **AES-XTS** (the Advanced Encryption Standard in XTS mode, a mode built for encrypting storage) on whole volumes. On Apple silicon Macs and Intel Macs with Apple's T2 security chip, every internal APFS (Apple File System) volume is encrypted even with FileVault off; the difference is who holds the key. Off, the volume key is protected only by the hardware UID inside the **Secure Enclave** (Apple's isolated security coprocessor). On, it is protected by the user's password *combined with* that hardware UID, and "encryption keys are never directly exposed to the CPU".

blocks.title: FileVault's key hierarchy on Apple silicon (simplified)

scenes.caption: The volume encryption key encrypts the data. It never changes when the password changes, so no re-encryption is needed.
FileVault off: the volume key is wrapped using only the hardware UID. Remove the SSD and it is useless elsewhere, but this Mac unlocks it at boot without a password.
FileVault on: the KEK needs the user's password combined with the UID. Turning it on is instant because the data was already encrypted; an anti-replay mechanism retires the old UID-only key.
Brute force must happen on this Mac, through the Secure Enclave, because the UID never leaves it. Deleting the volume key wipes the volume instantly.

blocks.code:
% fdesetup status
FileVault is On.
blocks.caption: Real output, read-only. fdesetup is also how scripts and MDM check status; turning FileVault on or off is not done here.

blocks.md: **Fleet FileVault.** Apple's [management page](https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/manage-filevault-with-device-management-dep0a2cb7686/web) describes requiring FileVault during Setup Assistant and escrowing the **personal recovery key** to the MDM service, so IT can unlock a Mac when someone forgets their password or leaves. It also notes that on macOS 26.4 or later FileVault is turned on during Setup Assistant by default; management is still used to escrow the key and stop users turning it off. A recovery key that only the departed employee knew is how companies lose their own data.

**Secure boot on Apple silicon.** Apple's [startup security page](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/startup-disk-security-policy-control-sec7d92dc49f/web) defines three policies:

- **Full Security** (default): like iPhone, the Mac requests a signature "personalized" with its chip ID (ECID, Exclusive Chip Identification) from Apple's signing server, so only current, Apple-signed macOS for *this* Mac boots, which also blocks rollback to old vulnerable versions.
- **Reduced Security**: accepts Apple's global signature, valid on any Mac, so older macOS versions can run and, if chosen, third-party kernel extensions; it gives no rollback protection. Set from recoveryOS.
- **Permissive Security**: set only with command-line tools, for users who accept "a much more insecure state": the boot chain still checks signatures but accepts locally signed boot objects such as a custom kernel.

The SSV, SIP and FileVault protect each other. Apple notes the system will not let a user turn off the signed system volume while FileVault is on, because a tampered OS could capture the password at next boot. A baseline should require Full Security, SIP, SSV and FileVault together, and MDM should report any Mac that drops one.

blocks.question: A Mac with Apple silicon has FileVault off. A thief removes nothing, just boots it. What protects the data?
options: The data is unencrypted
The thief needs the recovery key
The Secure Enclave refuses to boot
