The volume is encrypted, but the key is protected only by the hardware UID, so the Mac unlocks it at boot; only the login password stands in the way
blocks.explain: Apple: with FileVault off the volume key is protected only by the hardware UID. The disk is useless in another Mac, but on this Mac nothing cryptographic depends on the user's password.

blocks.question: Why does Full Security ask Apple's server for a personalised signature at install time?
options: To track users
Because Macs have no Secure Enclave
To speed up boot
So a signature works only for this Mac's chip, which blocks replaying an older, vulnerable signed macOS
blocks.explain: Personalised signatures include the ECID and are checked by the boot chain, giving protection against rollback that global signatures lack, per Apple's startup security page.

lessons.title: Case: Atomic Stealer and the paste-into-Terminal era

blocks.md:
Most Mac compromises a corporate SOC sees are not exploits. They are **information stealers**: malware that grabs passwords, browser cookies, keychain data and cryptocurrency wallets in minutes and sends them away. The best known is **Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS)**.

On 26 April 2023 the research team of Cyble, a threat intelligence company, [described AMOS](https://cyble.com/blog/threat-actor-selling-new-atomic-macos-amos-stealer-on-telegram/) being sold on Telegram as a service at USD 1,000 per month, including a web panel and a DMG installer. The sample they analysed was a `Setup.dmg` holding a Go program. Once run, it showed **a fake password prompt** to get the user's macOS password, then extracted keychain passwords (the **keychain** is macOS's encrypted store for passwords, keys and login tokens; each user gets a default one), files from Desktop and Documents, browser autofill, passwords, cookies and card data, and crypto wallets, zipped them, and sent them out.

blocks.title: How AMOS delivery moved as macOS defences moved

scenes.caption: 2023: fake app DMGs (Cyble's sample was Setup.dmg). The user opens an unsigned app, clicks past Gatekeeper and types their password into a fake dialog.
August 2024: Apple announces that macOS Sequoia removes the Control-click override, so an unnotarized app now needs a trip to System Settings. Fake DMGs keep circulating.
Early 2026: Microsoft notes earlier waves used DMGs and now tracks ClickFix pages telling users to paste a Terminal command; nothing is quarantined, so Gatekeeper is never asked. Dates simplified.
2026: macOS 26.4 adds a Terminal paste warning, pasteboard command blocking and AppleScript scanning (exact release timing simplified here).

blocks.md: **The 2026 chain.** Microsoft's [May 2026 analysis](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/06/clickfix-campaign-uses-fake-macos-utilities-lures-deliver-infostealers/) of ClickFix campaigns delivering AMOS, SHub and Macsync explains why delivery moved: app bundles opened through Finder may face Gatekeeper's code signing and notarization checks, but "scripts downloaded and launched directly through Terminal (for example, by using osascript or shell interpreters) don't undergo the same evaluation." Lure pages, including fake troubleshooting posts, told users to paste an encoded command. Microsoft describes the stages: a loader fetches an AppleScript payload and runs it in memory with `osascript` (the command-line runner for AppleScript, Apple's scripting language); the script asks for the user's password, checks it with `dscl . -authonly`, copies keychain databases (which then give up stored website passwords and Wi-Fi credentials), browser data and wallets, zips them under `/tmp`, uploads them with `curl`, and may add a LaunchAgent.

blocks.title: One ClickFix infection, with the evidence each step leaves

scenes.caption: A fake fix page tells the user to paste an encoded command. On macOS 26.4 or later a user who has not opened Terminal in 30 days and has no developer tools sees a warning.
The command fetches a script with curl and pipes it to osascript: no file, no Gatekeeper.
A dialog asks for the password; dscl -authonly checks it before the attacker uses it.
Keychain, browser and wallet files are zipped and uploaded; a LaunchAgent may be added.
ES exec events captured each child (curl, osascript, sh, dscl, zip) with command lines: a full trail if anyone collects it.

blocks.md: **Apple's answer.** On macOS 26.4 or later Apple's [Terminal and script protections](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/terminal-and-script-protections-sece3b202c4b/web) add three layers: a **paste warning** when someone who has not opened Terminal in 30 days and has no developer tools pastes from a browser, Messages, Mail or similar; **pasteboard command blocking**, where XProtect traces the process tree of a pasted command in any terminal, checks network artefacts against Apple's Safe Browsing service and can block known malware behaviour; and **AppleScript scanning** of every AppleScript and JXA (JavaScript for Automation) execution, even from memory. Note the paste warning deliberately skips developers, the people most likely to paste commands, so fleet detection still matters.

**Defender's view.**

- **Prevent**: user training on one rule (no legitimate fix asks you to paste a command into Terminal); keep macOS current for the 26.4 protections; restrict who has local admin.
- **Detect**: the process ancestry browser, Terminal, curl, osascript, dscl; `osascript` making network connections; zip archives in `/tmp` followed by an upload; new LaunchAgents (lessons 10 and 13). ATT&CK: [T1059.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002/) AppleScript, [T1056.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/002/) GUI Input Capture, [T1555.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/001/) Keychain.
- **Respond**: treat every credential on the Mac as stolen: reset the macOS and SSO passwords, revoke browser sessions and OAuth tokens (the access tokens apps keep after you sign in) (stolen cookies bypass MFA), rotate SSH and cloud keys, move crypto funds, then reimage.

Resetting the user's password is not enough after a stealer. Session cookies stolen from the browser let the attacker into SaaS apps without the password or MFA until those sessions are revoked server-side.

blocks.question: Why did stealer operators move from fake app DMGs to "paste this into Terminal"?
options: Terminal commands run as root automatically
DMGs no longer open on macOS
Commands typed by the user and scripts piped into osascript skip the quarantine-triggered Gatekeeper and notarization checks
Terminal disables XProtect
blocks.explain: Microsoft's analysis states it directly: scripts launched from Terminal don't undergo the Gatekeeper evaluation that app bundles opened from Finder may get, and Sequoia had made overriding Gatekeeper for apps harder.

blocks.question: A user ran an AMOS-style command an hour ago. Which response step is most often missed?
options: Reimaging the Mac
Changing the Wi-Fi password
Running Disk Utility
Revoking active browser sessions and tokens for SaaS apps, since stolen cookies work without the password
blocks.explain: Stealers take cookies and tokens as well as passwords. A password reset does not end an existing session; revoke sessions at the identity provider and in key SaaS apps.

lessons.title: Case: 3CX, a notarized app with a poisoned library

blocks.md:
What if the malicious app is *really* from the vendor, correctly signed and notarized? In March 2023 that happened to **3CX**, a business phone (VoIP, voice over IP) software company whose desktop app runs on Windows and macOS. The supply chain side (an earlier trojanised trading app, X_TRADER, on an employee's PC leading into 3CX's build environments) is a supply chain attack: the attacker compromised the vendor so its normal releases carried the malware. Here we follow the macOS evidence.

[Jamf Threat Labs](https://www.jamf.com/blog/3cx-supply-chain-attack/) reported that the compromised macOS builds contained a malicious library, `libffmpeg.dylib`, loaded dynamically at run time. At the time of their analysis the app "was signed by 3CX and notarized by Apple with the teamid 33CF4654HL"; Apple then revoked the notarized code.

blocks.title: How a trusted Mac app carried a backdoor

nodes.label:
3CX macOS build server
POOLRAT via LaunchDaemon

scenes.caption: Mandiant: credentials stolen via a trojanised X_TRADER let the attacker reach 3CX's build environments; the macOS build server was backdoored with POOLRAT (a macOS backdoor), persisting through Launch Daemons.
Builds from that server included a malicious libffmpeg.dylib inside the app bundle. Signed with 3CX's real Developer ID, so library validation saw the right Team ID.
The app was notarized: the automated scan found nothing it knew. Gatekeeper on customer Macs accepted it.
Installed through normal updates, the library wrote files under the app's Application Support folder and fetched a second stage, UpdateAgent, from attacker servers (Jamf).

blocks.md:
Every Mac control in lessons 2 to 5 behaved exactly as designed and still let it through: the signature was valid (3CX's own), library validation passed (same Team ID), notarization passed (unknown code), and XProtect had no signature yet. Mandiant's [investigation](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise/) also found the attacker's own persistence on the macOS **build server** used Launch Daemons, the T1543.004 technique from lesson 10, on the machine that should have been most protected.

Jamf published indicators of compromise: the second stage at `~/Library/Application Support/3CX Desktop App/UpdateAgent`, plus `.main_storage`, `.session-lock` and `config.json` in the same folder, and the SHA-1 hashes of the dylib and UpdateAgent.

blocks.code:
-- osquery hunt for 3CX exposure (not run here: no osquery on this Mac)
-- 1. Is the app present, and with which signer?
SELECT path, team_identifier, authority
FROM signature
WHERE path = '/Applications/3CX Desktop App.app';

-- 2. Any of Jamf's file indicators in any user's home?
SELECT path, size, mtime
FROM file
WHERE path LIKE '/Users/%/Library/Application Support/3CX Desktop App/%'
  AND filename IN ('UpdateAgent', '.main_storage', '.session-lock');
blocks.caption: Columns follow osquery's signature and file table definitions. The file table needs a path constraint with LIKE patterns as shown.

blocks.md:
**Response at fleet scale.** Jamf recommended blocking by Team ID to stop every version at once; the same works as a Santa Team ID rule or an EDR block. Then:

1. **Scope**: who had the app, which versions, and which Macs have the UpdateAgent indicator.
2. **Contain**: block Team `33CF4654HL` until the vendor ships a clean build; block known command-and-control domains.
3. **Eradicate**: remove the app and its Application Support folder; reimage Macs where the second stage ran.
4. **Learn**: an inventory of every Team ID in the fleet, built with the `signature` table, is what lets you answer "do we run this?" in minutes.

Signatures and notarization establish *origin*, not *innocence*. When the origin itself is compromised, detection has to come from behaviour (a phone app downloading and running a second-stage binary) and from fast, Team-ID-wide blocking.

blocks.question: Why did library validation not stop the malicious libffmpeg.dylib?
options: Library validation is off for Electron apps
The dylib was loaded by Gatekeeper
SIP was disabled on customer Macs
The dylib was signed as part of 3CX's own build with the same Team ID as the app
blocks.explain: Library validation refuses libraries from other teams. A compromised build pipeline signs the malicious library with the vendor's own identity, so the check passes.

blocks.question: Which single control would have stopped every trojanised 3CX version on your fleet fastest once the advisory came out?
options: A Team ID block rule (Santa, EDR or MDM) for 33CF4654HL
Waiting for an XProtect update
Turning on FileVault
Removing the quarantine attribute
blocks.explain: A Team ID rule matches every build signed by that developer, the approach Jamf recommended. Hash-based blocks miss other versions, and waiting for Apple leaves a window.

lessons.title: A Mac hardening baseline, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Put the course together as a baseline: a written list of settings every company Mac must have, checked automatically. The **macOS Security Compliance Project** ([mSCP](https://github.com/usnistgov/macos_security)) is the public starting point. It is a joint project of NIST and other US government IT security staff; you choose a benchmark, and it generates configuration profiles, DDM declarations, documentation and compliance scripts, with each rule mapped to NIST SP 800-53. Its rules include `os_sip_enable`, `os_gatekeeper_enable`, `system_settings_gatekeeper_override_disallow`, `os_authenticated_root_enable`, `system_settings_firewall_enable` and FileVault enforcement.

Before trusting a fleet report, check one Mac by hand. This script only reads state, uses no `sudo`, and changes nothing:

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Read-only Mac posture check: no sudo, changes nothing.
echo "macOS:      $(sw_vers -productVersion)"
echo "SIP:        $(csrutil status | sed 's/.*status: //')"
echo "SSV:        $(csrutil authenticated-root status | sed 's/.*status: //')"
echo "Gatekeeper: $(spctl --status)"
echo "FileVault:  $(fdesetup status)"

blocks.md:
**A baseline for a company Mac fleet**, collecting every lesson:

1. Organisation-owned Macs in Automated Device Enrollment, supervised, unenrollment prevented (lesson 14).
2. Full Security boot policy, SIP and SSV on; alert on any Mac that reports otherwise (lessons 6, 15).
3. FileVault on with escrowed recovery keys (lesson 15).
4. Gatekeeper on, override disallowed where the business allows; App Store and identified developers (lessons 3, 4).
5. OS and XProtect updates enforced with deadlines through DDM; automatic security responses on (lessons 5, 14).
6. An ES-based EDR or Santa deployed and pre-approved; PPPC grants limited to IT and security agents (lessons 7, 12).
7. Managed Login Items for your own agents; alert on all others (lesson 10).
8. Logs and ES events shipped off the Mac; detections for paste-and-run, dscl -authonly, new LaunchAgents and TCC grants (lessons 11, 13, 16).
9. A Team ID inventory so advisories can be answered in minutes (lesson 17).
10. Standard (non-admin) accounts for daily work, so a stolen password does not also unlock /Library.

**Where to practise, legally.** Everything in this course was run on a Mac its author owns, read-only. You can do the same:

- Build your own toy app and repeat lessons 2, 3, 9, 10, 11 and 12 in a scratch folder: `codesign`, `spctl`, `syspolicy_check`, `plutil`, `xattr`, `eslogger --list-events`, and `log show` on your own subsystem.
- For anything that needs `sudo`, disabling protections or running samples, use a throwaway macOS virtual machine. Apple documents [running macOS in a virtual machine on Apple silicon](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/virtualization/running-macos-in-a-virtual-machine-on-apple-silicon) with its Virtualization framework.
- Read mSCP's rule files to see how each control is checked and fixed, and try [osquery](https://osquery.io/) against your own Mac.
- Practise the investigation side on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and the security exercises at [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/).

Only test Macs you own or have written permission to test, and never run real malware outside an isolated VM.

A Mac is well defended when every control from this course is on, managed, and observed: on by default (SIP, SSV, XProtect), switched on and escrowed (FileVault), constrained by policy (Gatekeeper, PPPC, login items), and watched (Endpoint Security, logs, osquery). Most real compromises came through the gap between "on" and "watched".

blocks.question: Your fleet report says 4% of Macs show `SIP: disabled`. What is the right first response?
options: Ignore it: SIP is only for developers
Turn off Gatekeeper on those Macs
Treat each as a finding: identify why (developer exception or tampering), re-enable via recoveryOS, and check those Macs for kernel extensions or system modifications
Delete the MDM profile
blocks.explain: SIP can only be turned off from recoveryOS, so each case is a deliberate action by someone with physical or admin access. Some are legitimate developer exceptions; all need an owner and a check.

blocks.question: Which item on the baseline most directly limits damage when a stealer gets a user's password?
options: Firewall stealth mode
Turning on Bluetooth
Standard (non-admin) accounts for daily work
XProtect remediators
blocks.explain: With a standard account the stolen password cannot install LaunchDaemons, change system settings or approve system extensions. It still exposes the user's own data, which is why the session revocation from lesson 16 is needed too.
